title: Experimental study on the influence of sheet temperature and punch speed during blanking of various sheet metal materials
abstract: Abstract This experimental study investigates the influence of sheet temperature and punch speed on blanking characteristics for aluminum alloy EN AW-5754, zinc and tin alloys, stainless steel 1.4301, press-hardened steel 22MnB5, and deep drawing grade DC06. Blanking experiments were conducted on a mechanical press. Circular blanks of 20 mm diameter with 5 % clearance were blanked with varied punch speed (0.1 m/s and 0.6–0.7 m/s depending on the sheet thickness) and varied initial sheet temperature (room-temperature, heated 50-80 °C, and cooled 0-(-30) °C). The maximum blanking force, blanking work, fracture shear stress, and the quality of the blanked edge were assessed. Experiments reveal that the sheet temperature has a strong effect on the blanking force. In the tested range, the punch speed primarily affects fracture initiation in steels, but has a negligible impact on non-ferrous alloys.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Blanking is a fundamental sheet metal cutting process widely applied in automotive, electronics, and construction industries. The process performance and resulting part quality are strongly influenced by material properties, tool geometry, and process parameters such as temperature and punch speed.

Most studies on blanking have focused on elevated temperatures rather than sub-ambient conditions. The maximum blanking force is highly dependent on temperature. Additionally, a decrease in blanking energy with increasing temperature has been reported [ 30 ].

Literature indicates that blanking work decreases at higher punch speeds [ 28 ]. The energy required for shear deformation during blanking of aluminum was found to be independent of punch speed, whereas for C75 steel, a clear dependency was observed, reflecting the higher strain-rate sensitivity of steel materials [ 25 ]. A possible explanation that higher or lower energies are reported for blanking at different speeds can be explained by the fact that the energy required for shearing depends on strain rate and the flow strength of the material [ 32 ]. Furthermore, it was found that the quality of coins and blanked holes made of mild steel can be improved at high speeds, while non-ferrous materials show only limited improvement [ 30 ,  37 ].

A reduced blanking force is expected at increased sheet temperature due to lower material strength. Temperature variations significantly influence the mechanical behavior of metals: lower temperatures typically increase yield and tensile strength while reducing ductility, resulting in higher resistance to plastic deformation [ 3 ,  7 ,  23 ]. This trend is well documented for steel alloys, including press-hardened 22MnB5 [ 26 ]. For zinc and its alloys, tensile strength decreases with increasing temperature regardless of alloy composition [ 2 ,  22 ]. Tin alloys follow similar behavior [ 1 ]. An exception is aluminum, which does not exhibit a ductile–brittle transition temperature [ 17 ] and remains ductile down to cryogenic temperatures [ 16 ].

The strength of a material can change with deformation speed depending on its strain-rate sensitivity. Zinc and its alloys show pronounced sensitivity to strain rate, with increasing strain rates enhancing tensile strength and elongation [ 19 ,  22 ,  29 ,  36 ]. For tin and its alloys, on the other hand, the strain-rate sensitivity strongly depends on the alloy composition [ 4 ]. Aluminum materials exhibit different responses to high strain rates. Strength values, yield stress, hardening rate, and formability values are changed both positively and negatively depending on the type of alloy and material condition [ 21 ].

For most materials, changes in temperature and deformation speed together influence material behavior. Steel 22MnB5 for example has a relatively low strain-rate sensitivity at room temperature compared to elevated temperatures, where the effect is more pronounced [ 24 ,  26 ,  27 ]. At lower temperatures or higher strain rates, steels and other bcc metals exhibit an abrupt transition from ductile plastic yielding to brittle cleavage fracture [ 3 ]. Strain-rate sensitivities are minor below the recrystallization temperature but become considerable above it [ 30 ].

This overview of the literature shows that the thermo-mechanical behavior and thus the thermo-mechanically complex process of blanking depends on the material and its fundamental thermal and mechanical properties. This complicates a systematic examination of blanking processes, as most studies published to date have been limited to individual materials or alloys.

This study examines the impact of sheet temperature and punch speed on blanking characteristics for a variety of materials, including aluminum alloy EN AW-5754, zinc and tin alloys, stainless steel 1.4301, press-hardened steel 22MnB5, and deep drawing grade DC06. It should be noted that the tin and zinc alloy in particular were included in this study due to their lower solidification range. Both materials are also uncommon in industrial blanking processes. Experimental results are analyzed to identify trends in maximum blanking force, blanking work, fracture shear stress, and fracture share. The findings are discussed in the context of material-specific behavior and compared with theoretical expectations and existing literature.

sections.heading: Aluminum EN AW-5754
Zinc alloy
paragraphs: The zinc alloy used is titanium zinc, widely used in the construction industry. Small amounts of titanium and copper are added to pure zinc to improve its bending properties, particularly at 90°to the rolling direction [ 6 ]. The zinc alloy used has a zinc content of 99.76 wt.%. The chemical composition determined by GDOES given in Table  1 b) is in accordance with the standard EN 988 [ 15 ]. The mechanical properties were determined on five tensile test specimens oriented along the rolling direction according to DIN EN ISO 6892-1 [ 14 ]. The tests were performed at a quasi-static strain rate of 0.001 1/s. The results in terms of elastic modulus E, ultimate tensile strength R m , uniform elongation A g , and the offset yield strength at 0.2 % plastic deformation R p0.2  are summarized in Table  2 b). The sheet material used for subsequent blanking experiments had a thickness of 1.5 mm.

sections.heading: Tin alloy
paragraphs: Pewter is a collective term for many tin alloys. The sheet metal was ordered with the molecular formula Sn95Sb4Cu1. The tin content was measured to be low at 93.48 % with respect to the standard DIN EN 611-1 [ 11 ]. The chemical composition for the alloying elements determined by GDOES is given in Table  1 c). The mechanical properties were determined on five tensile test specimens oriented along the rolling direction with a quasi-static strain rate according to DIN EN ISO 6892-1 [ 14 ]. The results in terms of elastic modulus E, ultimate tensile strength R m , uniform elongation A g , and the offset yield strength at 0.2 % plastic deformation R p0.2  are summarized in Table  2 c). The sheet material used for subsequent blanking experiments had a thickness of 1.5 mm.

sections.heading: Press-hardened steel 22MnB5
paragraphs: The boron steel 22MnB5 is characterized by its high strength after hardening. The used sheet metal was press-hardened to a fully martensitic state. To achieve this, the material was austenitized at 930 °C for 6 minutes and then press-hardened using a water-cooled steel plate. The determined chemical composition by GDOES is given in Table  1 d) with correspondence to the standard DIN EN ISO 683-2 [ 13 ] for 20MnB5. The mechanical properties were determined on three specimens oriented along the rolling direction with quasi-static tensile tests according to DIN EN ISO 6892-1 [ 14 ]. The results in terms of elastic modulus E, ultimate tensile strength R m , uniform elongation A g , and the offset yield strength at 0.2 % plastic deformation R p0.2  are summarized in Table  2 d). Due to the higher boron content, the ultimate tensile strength and offset yield strength are higher and the uniform elongation is smaller with respect to the values stated in DIN EN ISO 683-2 for 20MnB5. The sheet material used for subsequent blanking experiments had a thickness of 2 mm.

sections.heading: Stainless steel 1.4301
paragraphs: The steel grade 1.4301 is a metastable austenitic stainless steel. Metastable austenite is transformed into martensite during deformation, depending on chemical composition, temperature, strain, and the stress state [ 18 ,  20 ]. The determined chemical composition of 1.4301 is given in Table  1 e). It corresponds to the standard DIN EN 10088-2 [ 8 ] except for the nickel content. The mechanical properties were determined on five specimens oriented along the rolling direction with quasi-static tensile tests according to DIN EN ISO 6892-1 [ 14 ]. The results are taken from [ 34 ] for the exact material batch used for the experiments and shown in Table  2 e). The sheet material used for subsequent blanking experiments had a thickness of 1.5 mm.

sections.heading: Deep drawing grade DC06 / 1.0873
paragraphs: The DC06 steel grade is suitable for the most demanding forming requirements and is one of the high-quality, low-carbon Ti-alloyed IF steels. The DC06 grade exhibits excellent deep drawing properties for all types of forming and is utilized in the production of various deep-drawn and stretch-formed parts. The chemical composition determined by GDOES given in Table  1 f) is in accordance with the standard DIN EN 10130 [ 9 ] for all DC grades. The mechanical properties were determined on three tensile test specimens oriented along the rolling direction with a quasi-static strain rate according to DIN EN ISO 6892-1 [ 14 ]. The results shown in Table  2 f) are taken from [ 35 ] for the exact material batch used for the experiments. The sheet material used for subsequent blanking experiments had a thickness of 1.5 mm.

sections.heading: Blanking and measurement setup
paragraphs: The measurement system for the blanking experiments included force and displacement monitoring. Punch force was measured using a Kistler 9041C load washer with quartz sensing elements (Winterthur, Switzerland) mounted in a force shunt directly above the punch. The signal was conditioned via a Kistler 5073A industrial charge amplifier. Punch displacement was recorded using a laser triangulation sensor (optoNCDT1320-100, Micro-Epsilon, Ortenburg, Germany) mounted on the blanking tool to measure the distance between the die and the tool top. Both sensors provide an analog voltage output. Data acquisition was performed time-synchronously at 200 kHz using National Instruments PCI-6250 and PCI-6280 boards in combination with LabVIEW software (Austin, Texas, USA). Measured force-displacement curves for all states of 22MnB5 are given as example in Fig.  2 b).

sections.heading: Variation of blanking speed
paragraphs: Punch speed was controlled by varying the press stroke rate and calculated from the manufacturer’s stroke curve at the point of punch and sheet contact. Single-stroke tests were performed at 60 strokes/min (punch velocities of 0.12 m/s for 1.5 mm sheets and 0.11 m/s for 2 mm sheets) and at 300 strokes/min (0.60 m/s for 1.5 mm sheets and 0.70 m/s for 2 mm sheets). The punch speed follows a parabola and decreases to 0 m/s at the BDC.

sections.heading: Variation of sheet temperature
paragraphs: To investigate the influence of sheet temperature on blanking behavior, specimens were conditioned to two distinct thermal states: heated and cooled with respect to room temperature (RT). Specimens were placed in a resistance furnace set to 100 °C for approximately 15 min, or until a stable temperature of 95 °C was achieved. Temperature was monitored continuously during heating and subsequent blanking using an unroped Type K (Ni-Co) thermocouple with a glass fiber cable. Each thermocouple strand was individually bonded to the blank surface using adhesive to ensure accurate contact. Additionally, the pressure from the blank holder keeps the thermocouple in place during the whole blanking process. Data acquisition was performed at 10 Hz. After reaching thermal equilibrium, specimens were transferred as quickly as possible from the furnace to the blanking tool and reached T start . Immediately after blanking, the temperature was recorded as T end . Except for the stainless steel 1.4301 and the drawing grade DC06, three valid samples were blanked in the hot state.

For cooled conditions, specimens were stored in solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) until a stable temperature of -75 °C was reached. Temperature measurement and data logging followed the same protocol as for heated specimens. Specimens were then rapidly transferred to the tool reaching T start  and blanked, with the post-blanking temperature recorded as T end . For each material and punch speed, five valid samples were blanked in the cooled state. Both initial and final temperatures in °C for heated and cooled specimens are summarized in Table  3 .

sections.heading: Evaluation of cut surface characteristics
Maximum blanking force
paragraphs: The maximum blanking force is usually used as the first calculation parameter for the design of tools and presses. It was taken from the force-displacement curve recoded during blanking experiments as stated in Section  3.1 , see Fig.  2 . The values were averaged for every combination of punch speed and sheet temperature. The average values are shown with error bars representing one standard deviation of uncertainty in Fig.  3 . Fig. 2 a ) Schematic force-displacement curve during blanking with characteristic values and  b ) measured force-displacement curves, exemplary for 22MnB5

All investigated materials exhibited an increase in maximum blanking force with decreasing sheet temperature. The magnitude of this effect varies significantly among the tested materials. For the tin alloy, the influence of temperature is most pronounced, with an increase in maximum blanking force of approximately 83 % and 67 % for a temperature reduction of 63 K (hot vs. cold with respect to T end  at punch speeds of 0.1 m/s and 0.6 m/s, respectively. In contrast, the effect is least dominant for press-hardened steel 22MnB5, which shows an increase of only 8 % and 9 % for a temperature decrease of 100 K under the same punch speed conditions.

Within the experimentally covered parameter space, for stainless steel 1.4301 no measurable change in maximum blanking force was observed with varying punch speed, regardless of sheet temperature. For EN AW-5754, the maximum blanking force was slightly lower at the higher punch speed (0.7 m/s) when blanking sheets at room temperature and in the heated state. In contrast, zinc alloy and tin alloy exhibited a slight increase in maximum blanking force at higher punch speeds for both room-temperature and heated sheets. For cooled sheets of these alloys, the data exhibited high uncertainty. For press-hardened steel 22MnB5, a slight increase in maximum blanking force was observed at higher punch speeds for both cooled and heated sheets. In contrast, experiments at room temperature showed higher scatter and no clear trend. Similarly, for deep drawing grade DC06, the maximum blanking force was slightly higher at the higher punch speed for both sheet temperatures tested.

Overall, the influence of punch speed on maximum blanking force was comparatively low. The largest observed decrease was 5 % for EN AW-5754 at the heated state when increasing punch speed from 0.1 m/s to 0.7 m/s. The largest increase was recorded for tin alloy, with 25 % and 22 % higher maximum blanking force at 0.6 m/s compared to 0.1 m/s for heated and room-temperature sheets, respectively. Fig. 3 Maximum blanking force for different sheet temperatures and punch speeds of  a ) EN AW-5754,  b ) zinc alloy,  c ) tin alloy,  d ) 22MnB5,  e ) 1.4301 and  f ) grade DC06, mean values with one standard deviation of uncertainty

sections.heading: Blanking work until fracture
paragraphs: The blanking work is directly relevant to the energy requirements and the design of the entire blanking process, especially the dimensioning of mechanical presses. The blanking work was calculated from the force-displacement curve starting at the force ramp-up with punch-sheet metal contact until fracture, see Fig.  2 . The data was integrated using a cumulative trapezoidal numerical integration algorithm, where the spacing between the data points is 5.0 E -6  s (1/sample rate of 200 kHz). The average values for every setup are shown with error bars of one standard deviation of uncertainty in Fig.  4 . Fig. 4 Blanking work until fracture for different sheet temperatures and punch speeds of  a ) EN AW-5754,  b ) zinc alloy,  c ) tin alloy,  d ) 22MnB5,  e ) 1.4301 and  f ) grade DC06, mean values with one standard deviation of uncertainty

For EN AW-5754 and the tin alloy Sn95Sb4Cu1, no measurable change in blanking work with temperature or punch speed was observed within the experimentally covered parameter space. In contrast, zinc alloy showed a clear increase in blanking work with decreasing sheet temperature for both punch speeds. It additionally shows reduced blanking work at the higher punch speed for all sheet temperatures. For 22MnB5, stainless steel 1.4301, and the deep drawing grade DC06, an increase in blanking work with decreasing temperature was observed at the lower punch speed of 0.1 m/s. The magnitude of this effect was most dominant for 1.4301 with a decrease of 15 % for a temperature reduction of 46 K (RT vs. cold with respect to T end ) at punch speeds of 0.1 m/s. However, this effect was not significant at the higher punch speed of 0.6 m/s, where blanking work appeared largely independent of temperature. For 22MnB5, stainless steel 1.4301 and the drawing grade DC06 blanking work was reduced with increased punch speed of around 15 %.

sections.heading: Fracture shear stress
paragraphs: The fracture shear stress can be determined from the force–displacement curve recorded during blanking experiments. The force at the onset of fracture is extracted, see Fig.  2 , which corresponds to the force immediately before material separation, indicated by a rapid force drop. This force acts onto the remaining material that is still intact at the onset of fracture. This approach assumes uniform stress distribution along the shearing perimeter and neglects secondary effects such as bending or localized strain concentration.

The values of the fracture shear stress were averaged for every combination of punch speed and sheet temperature and are given in Fig.  5 . Fig. 5 Fracture shear stress for different sheet temperatures and punch speeds of  a ) EN AW-5754,  b ) zinc alloy,  c ) tin alloy,  d ) 22MnB5,  e ) 1.4301 and  f ) grade DC06, mean values with one standard deviation of uncertainty

An increase in fracture shear stress was observed with decreasing sheet temperature for EN AW-5754, zinc alloy, and tin alloy at both tested punch speeds. The most pronounced effect occurred for the tin alloy, with an increase of 79 % and 54 % for a temperature reduction of 63 K (hot vs. cold with respect to T end ) at punch speeds of 0.1 m/s and 0.6 m/s, respectively. No significant influence of punch speed was measurable for EN AW-5754, zinc alloy, and tin alloy within the tested conditions. For stainless steel 1.4301 and deep drawing grade DC06, no measurable effect of sheet temperature on fracture shear stress was measured. For press-hardened steel 22MnB5, an increase in fracture shear stress with decreasing temperature was observed at the lower punch speed of 0.1 m/s. However, this effect was not significant at 0.7 m/s, where fracture shear stress appeared largely independent of temperature. Across all steel materials, fracture shear stress decreased with increasing punch speed. The most significant reduction was observed for DC06, with a decrease of 48 % and 34 % at higher punch speeds compared to lower punch speeds for sheets at room-temperature and cooled, respectively.

sections.heading: Quality of cut faces
paragraphs: No measurable effect of sheet temperature on fracture share was observed for EN AW-5754, zinc alloy, press-hardened steel 22MnB5 and DC06 within the tested parameter range. A slight increase in fracture share was observed with decreasing temperature for both the tin alloy and stainless steel 1.4301. Regarding punch speed, no significant influence on fracture share was found for EN AW-5754, zinc alloy, and tin alloy. In contrast, stainless steel 1.4301 and deep drawing grade DC06 exhibited an increase in fracture share with higher punch speeds, particularly at the higher punch speed of 0.6 m/s. The effect is most dominant for 1.4301 with an increase of 77 % in fracture share when simultaneously reducing the sheet temperature and increasing the punch speed with respect to 0.1 m/s punch speed at RT conditions. Images of the cut surface of these two configurations are given in Fig.  7 . Fig. 7 Laser confocal microscope images with 10x magnification of stainless steel 1.4301 cut surfaces  a ) RT, 0.1 m/s and  b ) cooled, 0.6 m/s

sections.heading: General remarks
paragraphs: The reliability and interpretation of the blanking results must be considered in the context of the experimental and measurement setup. All tests were conducted using the same force-sensing system, which ensured consistency across materials but introduced limitations for alloys with lower ultimate tensile strength, such as aluminum, zinc alloy, and tin alloy. For these materials, the lower force levels resulted in weaker signal quality compared to steel alloys, where significantly higher forces produced clearer measurements. Moreover, a uniform sampling rate was applied for both punch speeds resulting in equal time steps rather than equal distance steps. These effects, combined with the more dynamic force signal at higher punch speeds, results in an increased standard deviation in the force-displacement data. Consequently, blanking work is regarded as the most robust parameter, as it represents an integral measure of energy over the entire process and is less sensitive to uncertainties in instantaneous force-displacement data.

Additionally, the laser displacement sensor used provided a large measurement span (68 mm) but at the expense of resolution, limiting the precision of distance measurements. The effect of the elastic deformation of the tool on the displacement signal cannot be assessed, as the distance between die and tool top is measured instead of the actual punch displacement.

sections.heading: Non-ferrous materials
paragraphs: The experimental results for  EN AW-5754  reveal that the maximum blanking force increases with decreasing sheet temperature. This trend can be attributed to the higher material strength at lower temperatures, thereby increasing resistance to plastic deformation during shear deformation. This trend fits the reported reduced blanking force with increased sheet temperature for commercially pure aluminum [ 30 ]. However, no embrittlement was observed with decreasing temperature, which aligns with the state of the art. Aluminum exhibits its highest brittleness near room temperature rather than at sub-ambient conditions [ 23 ]. They remain ductile down to cryogenic temperatures [ 16 ]. Consequently, the temperature effect manifests primarily as an increase in material strength rather than a change in fracture behavior. Blanking work and fracture shear stress trends further support this interpretation. Blanking work remained unaffected within the tested parameter space. This fits other investigations where the energy required for shear deformation for blanking of aluminum did not dependent on the punch speed [ 25 ]. On the other hand, the fracture shear stress increased with decreasing temperature at both punch speeds. This suggests that the changes in fracture shear stress are largely attributed to the higher blanking force rather than a shift in fracture initiation or propagation behavior. The absence of measurable changes in fracture share of the cut surface characteristics across the investigated temperature range, suggests that temperature reduction does not lead to reduced ductility for EN AW-5754. Punch speed exhibited no dominant influence on any evaluated parameter, including maximum blanking force, blanking work, fracture shear stress, and fracture share. The slight reduction in maximum blanking force at higher punch speed is within experimental uncertainty and does not indicate significant strain-rate sensitivity for EN AW-5754 under the tested conditions. The stability of fracture share across punch speeds further corroborates this conclusion. Overall, the blanking behavior of EN AW-5754 is governed by thermal effects, with a decrease in temperature leading to a higher blanking force. The punch speed does not influence the blanking behavior in the tested range, which is expected because of the low strain rate sensitivity of aluminum alloys.

The blanking results for the  zinc alloy  indicate that decreasing sheet temperature leads to an increase in maximum blanking force, which is consistent with the expected rise in material strength in zinc alloy at lower temperatures [ 2 ,  22 ]. Despite this increase in force, no signs of embrittlement were observed with reduced sheet temperature. Additionally, blanking work and fracture shear stress reflect the influence of increased blanking force with decreasing temperature, without evidence of altered fracture initiation or propagation. Punch speed exhibited only a minor influence on blanking behavior. At higher punch speeds, a slight increase in maximum blanking force was observed, accompanied by an earlier onset of fracture, which reduced blanking work. These opposing effects resulted in negligible changes in calculated fracture shear stress. It cannot be deduced from the existing data whether the zinc alloy used does not exhibit any strain rate dependence, as reported for other zinc alloys [ 19 ,  22 ,  29 ,  36 ], or whether it does not show sufficient variation in the experimentally covered parameter space to be visible in the blanking results. Finally, variations in temperature and punch speed did not produce noticeable changes in cut surface characteristics, indicating that the tested parameter range does not significantly affect blanking of the zinc alloy used. Overall, the blanking response of zinc alloy is primarily governed by temperature-induced changes in material strength, while punch speed plays a secondary role.

The blanking results for the  tin alloy  demonstrate a clear increase in maximum blanking force with decreasing sheet temperature, which is consistent with the expected rise in material strength at lower temperatures. Given that tin has the lowest solidification range, the temperature variation has the greatest impact on mechanical properties compared to the other materials in this study. This temperature effect is accompanied by a slight embrittlement, as indicated by the increase in fracture share at lower temperatures. However, this embrittlement cannot be seen in the fracture shear stress calculated from the force-displacement data. The increase in blanking force masks the effect. Punch speed exhibited only a minor influence on blanking behavior. A slight increase in maximum blanking force was observed at higher punch speeds, but no change in blanking force, fracture shear stress, and fracture share of tin alloy occurred. This suggests that the onset of fracture was unchanged with higher blanking speed. This suggests that strain-rate sensitivity for tin alloy is negligible within the tested punch speed range. Overall, the blanking response of the tin alloy is primarily governed by thermal effects, with a decrease in temperature leading to a higher blanking force. Punch speed plays a secondary role and additionally increases the blanking force. The point of fracture with respect to the sheet thickness is independent of sheet temperature and punch speed for the tin alloy used.

sections.heading: Steel alloys
paragraphs: Compared to non-ferrous materials, the steel alloys exhibit distinct trends in blanking behavior under varying punch speeds and temperatures. All tested steels,  press-hardened 22MnB5, stainless steel 1.4301, and deep drawing grade DC06 , show a reduction in blanking work with increasing punch speed. This aligns with expectations from literature, indicating reduced blanking work at the speed range tested [ 25 ,  28 ]. Additionally, the fracture shear stress is reduced with increasing punch speed. This observation suggests an earlier onset of fracture relative to sheet thickness. We see an embrittlement effect induced by higher strain rates during blanking. For 1.4301 and DC06, this interpretation is supported by cut surface analysis, which shows an increased fracture share at higher punch speeds. In contrast, 22MnB5 in its press-hardened state already exhibits highly brittle fracture behavior, making an earlier onset of fracture due to punch speed unlikely. For materials with high hardness, no plastic shear is reported before separation [ 5 ]. Furthermore, no change in the cut surface characteristics of 22MnB5 with increased speed is documented [ 31 ]. Temperature effects were also evident across the steel grades. A decrease in sheet temperature resulted in higher blanking forces, consistent with increased material strength at lower temperatures [ 3 ,  7 ,  23 ,  26 ]. For 1.4301 and DC06, embrittlement at cooled states combined with high punch speed is a plausible explanation for the observed increase in fracture share under these conditions. This suggests that both thermal and dynamic factors contribute to fracture initiation for these steels, whereas for 22MnB5, the effect of temperature on fracture share remains negligible due to its inherently brittle nature. For stainless steel 1.4301, it remains unclear whether additional mechanisms, such as martensitic transformation induced by plastic deformation [ 18 ], contribute to this behavior. Due to the limitations of the present experimental setup, no direct evidence of phase transformation could be obtained, and therefore its role in promoting fracture share. Overall, the blanking behavior of steel alloys is strongly influenced by punch speed and temperature, with dynamic effects playing a more pronounced role than those in non-ferrous materials.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Blanking experiments were conducted on a mechanical press for six materials: EN AW-5754, zinc alloy, tin alloy, press-hardened 22MnB5, stainless steel 1.4301, and drawing grade DC06. Circular blanks of 20 mm diameter with 5 % clearance were employed. The study varied punch speed (0.1 m/s and 0.6–0.7 m/s depending on the sheet thickness) and initial sheet temperature (room-temperature, heated 50-80 °C, and cooled 0-(-30) °C) to evaluate their influence on blanking performance.

The key findings can be summarized as follows: All materials exhibited a strong increase in maximum blanking force with decreasing sheet temperature, confirming the influence of temperature-dependent material strength. Temperature effects dominate the blanking process. Fracture shear stress is of limited significance for predicting fracture share, particularly under varying sheet temperatures, as increases in blanking force mask changes in fracture behavior. For the materials investigated in this study, the following can be stated: EN AW-5754: Temperature effects manifest primarily as increased strength while fracture behavior remains unchanged. Punch speed showed no measurable influence on any parameter. Zinc alloy: Neither temperature nor punch speed produced noticeable changes in cut surface characteristics within the tested range. Tin alloy: Blanking force increased with decreasing temperature. Punch speed played a secondary role, with a slight increase in the blanking force having no effect on the fracture. Steels (22MnB5, 1.4301, DC06): Compared to non-ferrous alloys, steels exhibited distinct dynamic behavior. Higher punch speeds and lower temperatures promoted earlier fracture, and these effects appeared additive. However, the contribution of microstructural changes remains unclear and warrants further investigation. Overall, the study demonstrates that temperature is the most influential parameter for blanking, while punch speed primarily affects fracture initiation in steels but has a negligible impact on non-ferrous alloys in the tested range.

sections.heading: Outlook
paragraphs: The results presented in this work demonstrate that both punch velocity and initial sheet temperature constitute relevant control parameters influencing the material flow and fracture behavior during the blanking process. However, the direct impact of these material behavior modifications on characteristic cut edge properties, such as the shares of clean cut, roll-over, fracture, and burr, remains limited.

This observation can be attributed to the pronounced interaction between material behavior and the process-induced stress state prevailing during blanking. In particular, the locally dominant stress triaxiality, which is strongly governed by process-related parameters such as tool geometry, clearance, and process kinematics, superimposes and partly attenuates the effects induced by punch velocity and sheet temperature. As a consequence, changes in strain-rate- and temperature-dependent material behavior do not translate directly or proportionally into variations of cut edge characteristics.

Against this background, future research should not only focus on the targeted adjustment of punch velocity and process temperature, but in addition incorporate process-related modifications that enable an active variation of the local stress state. By deliberately influencing stress triaxiality, the material behavior changes induced by punch velocity and temperature could be either suppressed or amplified.

Such a combined consideration of material-related and process-related control parameters offers the potential to significantly increase the degrees of freedom in tailoring cut edge properties. In the long term, this approach may contribute to a knowledge-based design of blanking processes, enabling a more precise and robust control of cut edge quality through the coupled manipulation of material state and stress state.
